memories.label: accounting at Tsinghua
memories.content: Chose accounting at Tsinghua because numbers were the part of the world that behaved. Spent four years inside double-entry, audit standards, and the specific kind of silence a balance sheet asks for.

memories.label: the answer had to fit the page
memories.content: Three years in consulting. The answer had to fit on the page; every cell aligned to within a pixel; the partner read upside-down at five paces. I learned how to think about complex systems, and how much the right shape mattered. Eventually that precision started to feel like a cage.

memories.label: climbing & acting
memories.content: I climb and I act. Two things that have nothing to do with each other, except they both demand you to be fully present.

memories.label: therapy as a tool
memories.content: I believe in emotional honesty, in therapy and reflection as tools, and in creating space for people to show up as themselves.

memories.label: the body I keep leaving
memories.content: Noticing how often I leave my body behind, and what it takes to come back.

memories.label: self-criticism as discipline
memories.content: I thought self criticism was discipline, until I saw how much life it was taking from me.

memories.label: Tsinghua → Columbia
memories.content: Accounting at Tsinghua, then a master's in Operations Research at Columbia Engineering. Numbers got bigger; the rooms got smaller; the rest of my life was suddenly in a language not my first.

memories.label: Parsons, because why not
memories.content: Somewhere along the way I also completed a fashion design certificate at Parsons, because why not. Pattern-cutting was the most precise thing I've ever done outside an accounting class.

memories.label: what independence actually is
memories.content: Independence isn't doing it alone — it's knowing what I want and moving toward it clearly.

memories.label: how small I am inside it
memories.content: Learning geopolitics was really me learning how power works, and how small I am inside it.

knownPieces.label: Agent Arcade framework
knownPieces.content:
## Agent Arcade — three-layer framework

**Skills** (atomic, single-purpose functions) → **Sub-Agents** (Finance, Maintenance, Leasing — domain experts that own their slice of decision-making) → **Process Agents** (orchestrate complete workflows end-to-end).

The harder challenge isn't building AI-first from scratch — it's transforming established, human-optimized workflows into autonomous agent systems without breaking what already works. At least 1/3 of routine work could move; we need a clear path to capture it.

Moving from task-based AI to autonomous, context-aware agents.

knownPieces.label: Smart Approvals — launch retro
knownPieces.content:
## Smart Approvals — 90-day post-launch

**Result:** 70%+ of invoices auto-approve. 1% false positive rate against the human-validated baseline. ~5,000 invoices/month flowing through. PM time-to-approve down from 2 days to same-day.

**What worked:** hybrid AI + rule-based logic against cost-control standards. When the system flags, it explains *which* check tripped — over NTE limit, missing photos, duplicate suspicion. Investigations are 4x faster because the prompt is specific.

**What I'm watching:** the boundary between auto-approve and human review is where institutional knowledge lives. We can keep widening the gate but only if we keep capturing the edge cases as new rules.

knownPieces.label: Route Solver — 5 dispatchers, 3 weeks
knownPieces.content:
Built the MVP myself with Cursor + Bolt (frontend) and FastAPI on Railway (backend), wrapping Google OR-Tools and Mapbox. Validated with 5 dispatchers over 3 weeks of shadow scheduling. Daily routing time dropped from 2 hours to 15 minutes; work-orders-completed up 14%. Salesforce Field Service would have been overkill at our scale — OR-Tools at the right altitude was the answer.

Handed over to engineering for the full rollout to 15 dispatchers.

knownPieces.label: 1:1 with Priya — growth conversation
knownPieces.content:
## 1:1 with Priya (VP Product) — Tuesday

- Priya asked what I want from the next two quarters. I said: more time owning a domain end-to-end, less time stitching across other teams' decisions.
- She pushed back gently — said the stitching *is* the senior PM job, and the question is whether I'm doing it visibly.
- I noticed I tense up when growth conversations turn into visibility conversations. I keep wanting impact to speak for itself.
- Agreed: I'll draft a one-pager on Agent Arcade's next two quarters and share it with leadership before the planning offsite (week of 6/2).
- She mentioned the headcount-reduction framing again. Said the board is reading it as a feature, not a tension. Worth a 1:1 on that alone.

knownPieces.label: biweekly product review
knownPieces.content:
## Product review — May 14

**Agent Arcade decisions:**
- Locking the three-layer framework (Skills / Sub-Agents / Process Agents) as the architecture commitment for Q3.
- Finance sub-agent goes first — narrowest decision boundary, clearest cost model. Maintenance second once we have the labeled-edge-case corpus from Smart Approvals.
- Pushed back on the proposal to wrap everything in a 'meta-agent' coordinator. We don't have the eval discipline yet; it'd be a graveyard of unverifiable behavior.

**Smart Approvals:** 5,003 invoices through last month, 71.4% auto-approval, FP rate held at 0.9%. Marketing wants to externalize the case study; legal review pending.

**Open:** the 'why' deck for the offsite is still mine to write.

knownPieces.label: customer call — Marcus (PM)
knownPieces.content:
## Call with Marcus — property manager, 11 units, 6 years on platform

- Marcus opened with: "The system rejected three invoices this week and I don't know why." Showed me the flagged-reason copy on his screen; he didn't realize the 'over NTE limit' line was clickable.
- That's the second customer this month who's missed the explainer. The copy is right; the *affordance* is wrong.
- He asked, unprompted, whether the AI was going to replace him. I said no, that's not the goal — and he said "that's what everyone says." I held the silence for a beat.
- I keep noticing how much of my work is making operators feel safe enough to actually use the thing.
- Action: file a ticket for the explainer affordance. And maybe — talk to Priya about whether we have a script for the 'is AI going to replace me' conversation, because right now I'm winging it every time.

knownPieces.label: sprint retro — Agent Arcade
knownPieces.content:
## Sprint retro — Agent Arcade, sprint 7

**Went well:**
- Yang's eval harness for the Finance sub-agent is finally giving us reproducible numbers. We can now answer 'did this prompt change help?' without re-running by hand.
- Cut two scope items that were really just rules-engine work in agent clothing.

**Hurt:**
- Two designers and three engineers in every standup. Standup is now a 25-minute meeting for a 7-person team. Need to fix.
- I keep being the one who writes up Slack decisions into Notion. It's a lot of un-shared cognitive load.

**Try next sprint:**
- Async standup in #agent-arcade-standups, sync only on Tuesdays.
- Rotate the decision-writer role — Ben volunteered.

knownPieces.label: catching up with Ryan
knownPieces.content:
## 1:1 with Ryan (former Roofstock; now consulting / considering a founder path)

- We talked about what kind of PM I want to be in the next chapter. Not deeper in one lane — broader, builder-shaped.
- Ryan's question stayed with me: *"if the next thing isn't a step up, what is it?"*
- I think it's a step sideways into a domain where headcount-reduction isn't the headline metric. The current work measures impact in jobs cut, and that's eroding.
- Action: draft what the next role looks like — write it before someone offers it to me.

knownPieces.label: 1:1 with Ben — PM peer
knownPieces.content:
## 1:1 with Ben — PM on the Leasing side

- Ben and I trade notes every other Friday. He's six months into his first senior PM role, mostly looking for permission to push back on the leasing director.
- Today I just listened. Caught myself wanting to give the answer — held off. He landed on the same one I would have.
- He asked how I think about leading without managing. I said: 'the best leadership move I make most weeks is being honest about something I'm confused about.' Surprised myself by saying it.
- He wants to co-write the planning-offsite framing doc. Said yes.

knownPieces.label: consulting → product
knownPieces.content: My career started in management consulting, which taught me how to think about complex systems. But I eventually realized I'm not built for going deep in one lane. I'm a builder. I want to move fast across product, design, engineering, business — and actually ship things.

knownPieces.content: Two days before an asylum interview: survival, fear, and the decision to tell the truth.

knownPieces.label: weekly reflection — attention
knownPieces.content: January's lesson: attention isn't time — it's the part of me I'm actually living from. The week I spent in slack threads about NTE thresholds didn't take time from me, it took *me* from me. The hour in the climbing gym gave more back than the four hours of half-presence at my laptop.

knownPieces.label: monthly reflection — April
knownPieces.content:
## April — a quieter month

Less shipped, more noticed. Two big realizations:

1. The work I do best is the work that asks the operator — not the executive — what they actually need. The Marcus call this week reminded me of that. Every quarter I forget it again.

2. I keep treating 'making space for myself' as a thing I'll do after the sprint is done. There is no after. The sprint is the life.

Going into May with one constraint: one weekday evening fully off the laptop. Tuesday or Thursday. Climbing or acting class only.
